title: Fix the eleven posted bridges, in public order
stance: Publish the county bridge list, fix the worst first, and post the date each one reopens.
commitments: Publish the inspection score for all 64 county bridges within 90 days|Fix the eleven load-posted bridges worst-first, with the order posted on this site and the county's|Stop starting new road projects in a district until its posted bridges are on a funded schedule|Report every quarter at an evening commission meeting
cost: About $9.4 million over four years, most of it state bridge aid the county already qualifies for and has not applied for since 2019. The county share is roughly $1.1 million.
measure: Posted bridges in District 2: eleven today, five by the end of 2028, none by 2030|The school bus detour on Pell Orchard Road ends|Every bridge's score is on the county site, not in a binder at the road office
summary: Eleven bridges in District 2 carry a weight limit today. School buses and milk trucks drive around three of them.
body:
The Pell Orchard Road bridge has been posted at five tons since 2021. The school bus from Sexton Ridge adds eleven minutes each way going around it, and so does every milk truck that serves the farms on the far side.

The county has an inspection score for every bridge it owns. It is not secret, but it is not published either, and the order in which bridges get fixed has never been explained in public.

I will put the list on the county website, fix the worst first, and tell you when each one will reopen. If the order changes, the reason goes on the list too.

title: Keep the health office open until 7 pm, twice a week
stance: Two evenings a week at the county health office, so nobody loses a shift to get a shot or a test.
commitments: Open the county health office until 7 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays|Move one nurse position from the day schedule to the evening schedule; no new hires in year one|Run a monthly Saturday clinic at the Hollin Cross Grange|Publish wait times and visits for the evening hours every month
cost: About $84,000 a year in shift differential and building costs, found inside the current health budget by ending the second downtown lease.
measure: Evening visits counted and posted monthly|Fewer missed appointments for school vaccinations in August|A decision in public after one year on whether to keep it
summary: The county health office closes at 4:30. For most people who work in the district, that means losing pay to get a vaccine or a test.
body:
Most of the people I talked to on doors in Tannery Flats and Quillon Mills work first shift at the plants or the hospital in Marrow. The health office closes at 4:30.

Two late evenings a week is not a new program. It is the same office, open when people can get there. If after a year the evenings are empty, we will say so and change course.

title: Bring broadband to the last 1,900 addresses
stance: Use the federal and state money already on the table to finish the job on the ridge and in the orchards.
commitments: Map every address in District 2 without a 100 Mbps option, and publish the map|Apply for the state last-mile grant with the two co-ops that already serve the county|Put county right-of-way and poles on the table at cost, not as a revenue source|Hold a public meeting in each affected precinct before any contract is signed
cost: The state grant covers up to 75 percent. The county match, about $1.8 million, comes from the federal recovery money that is still unspent.
measure: Unserved addresses in District 2: about 1,900 today, under 300 by the end of 2029|The map is updated every six months, in public
summary: About 1,900 homes and farms in District 2, mostly in Pell Orchard and Sexton Ridge, still have no wired internet worth the name.
body:
On Sexton Ridge, a student doing homework drives to the Hollin Cross library parking lot. That is not a figure of speech; I have met three of them.

The money exists. What has been missing is a county that applies for it, works with the co-ops instead of waiting for a national carrier, and tells people where their road is on the list.

title: Put the county checkbook online
stance: Every county payment over $5,000, posted monthly, searchable, with the vendor's name.
commitments: Post every county payment over $5,000 each month, with vendor, department and purpose|Post the full draft budget thirty days before the vote, not five|Hold the budget hearing in the evening, in the district, with a remote option|Stop approving contracts on the consent agenda without a line of explanation
cost: Staff time in the treasurer's office; the accounting system already exports the data. No new software purchase.
measure: The first monthly checkbook file is posted within six months|Budget drafts are online thirty days before every vote
summary: The county spends about $112 million a year. Right now you have to file a records request to see where most of it goes.
body:
I have filed those requests myself. They take weeks, and the answer arrives as a scanned printout.

The county's accounting software exports a spreadsheet in about a minute. Posting it every month is a policy decision, not a technology project.

title: Two more licensed child care centers by 2029
stance: Clear the zoning and building rules that keep centers out of the district, and lend the county's empty buildings.
commitments: Change county zoning so licensed child care is allowed in every commercial and agricultural-commercial zone|Offer the closed Quillon Mills annex and the old Fallowmere ranger station at a dollar a year to licensed providers|Waive county permit fees for child care renovations|Report the waiting list numbers from the county's two existing centers every quarter
cost: Waived permit fees, roughly $30,000 a year, and the upkeep the county already pays on the two empty buildings.
measure: Licensed slots in District 2: 118 today, at least 220 by 2029|The waiting list at the two existing centers is posted and shrinking
summary: District 2 has 118 licensed child care slots and a waiting list of more than 200 children.
body:
The two centers in the district both have waiting lists longer than their enrollment. Parents in Ashby Ford drive their children to Marrow before their own shift starts.

The county cannot run a child care center, and it should not try. It can stop making it hard to open one.

title: A flood plan for Tannery Flats that people can read
stance: Finish the Wren River flood study, publish it, and make the buyout offer voluntary and fair.
commitments: Finish and publish the Wren River flood study the county paid for in 2023|Hold three evening meetings in Tannery Flats before any plan is adopted|Keep any buyout voluntary, at pre-flood value, with relocation help|Raise the Tannery Road culverts before the next spring melt
cost: The culvert work is about $640,000 and is in the road budget already. Buyouts would be 75 percent federally funded, and only if residents choose them.
measure: The flood study is public within 120 days|The Tannery Road culverts are raised by spring 2028
summary: Tannery Flats has flooded three times since 2019. The county paid for a flood study in 2023 that has never been released.
body:
I have stood in four basements in Tannery Flats where the waterline is still on the wall.

The study exists. People who live in the floodplain should read it before the commission does, not after.

title: Hold commission meetings in the evening
stance: Meet at 6:30 pm, stream every meeting, and keep the video and minutes in one place.
commitments: Move regular commission meetings from 9:30 am to 6:30 pm|Stream every meeting and archive the video next to the agenda and minutes|Rotate one meeting a quarter into each district|Allow public comment by video for anyone who cannot travel
cost: About $12,000 for a camera kit and the streaming service, and evening pay for two clerks.
measure: Every meeting is streamed and archived within a week|Public comment numbers are posted with the minutes
summary: The commission meets at 9:30 on Tuesday mornings, in a room most of the county has never seen.
body:
If you work, you cannot come to a 9:30 am meeting. That is most of the people the commission works for.

Evening meetings are normal in counties our size. So is a video archive. Neither one needs a study.
